# Section 11: Financial Recommendation

The evidence supports one recommendation with three parts: investment analysis under Philippine equity exposure should monitor the peso and the 10-year yield, should treat a month in which the peso weakens and the yield rises together as a reason to review risk, and should not rest decisions on the other regressors studied. The two prices are the only ones that stayed significant in every linear fit and in both logistic models, whereas the oil association depended on March 2020, the joint significance of the global factors depended on the covariance estimator, and the domestic macroeconomic indicators were not jointly significant. Our recommendation is therefore a way of managing exposure and not a forecast of returns, because the estimates are contemporaneous associations from a single sample and do not establish causation.

The USD/PHP exchange rate should be monitored first, since it has the strongest association with the market: a 1 percent depreciation goes with a monthly return about 2.0 percentage points lower and multiplies the odds of a crash month by 2.65. A sustained weakening may signal declining investor confidence or foreign capital outflows, and it raises the cost of imported inputs and foreign-currency obligations, which cuts into earnings [@bartov_firm_1994]. The index-level result cannot show which holdings carry that exposure, so a depreciation should lead the investor to examine the companies held, in particular their foreign-currency liabilities, reliance on imported materials and dependence on foreign capital, and to consider reducing the weight of the most exposed.

The Philippine 10-year government bond yield should be monitored alongside it. A 10 basis point rise goes with a return 0.35 to 0.41 percentage points lower, a smaller but consistent effect that works through two channels. Higher yields lower the present value of expected earnings [@campbell_dividend-price_1988] and make government securities more attractive relative to shares, because they pay a return with less risk. They also raise borrowing costs, which fall hardest on firms with substantial debt or dependence on external financing [@bernanke_inside_1995], so the debt and refinancing profile of each holding deserves attention when yields climb. The policy rate need not be tracked separately, since it carried no signal beyond the yield and the peso.

Crude oil prices should not serve as a standalone indicator of PSEi performance. The association between WTI and returns lost significance under HC3 errors and once March 2020 was controlled, so the sample does not support using oil movements as a primary basis for anticipating returns or for investment decisions. The S&P 500, the VIX and the domestic indicators of inflation, M3 growth and manufacturing production are in the same position: the data leave them inconclusive, not irrelevant, and so give no basis for a rule.

The strongest case for action arises when the two signals coincide. Applying the estimated odds ratios to the sample frequencies, a month with a 1 percent depreciation and a 10 basis point rise in the yield would cut the chance of an up month from 50 percent to about 23 percent and raise the chance of a crash month from 22 percent to about 48 percent, illustrative figures and not forecasts. In such a month the investor should reassess portfolio risk, favor companies with strong balance sheets, manageable debt, stable cash flows and resilient business models, and diversify beyond equities, since equity markets tend to move together more closely in downturns [@longin_extreme_2001]. Because bond prices fall when yields rise, the added fixed-income exposure is better held in short-dated government securities than in long-dated ones.

In conclusion, we stress that these indicators supplement, and do not replace, the analysis of company fundamentals and the broader economic outlook. The models leave a large share of return variation unexplained, describe only the same month and rest on 21 crash months in one sample from 2018 to 2025, so the peso and the yield indicate when to review exposure and not when to buy or sell. We recommend therefore to use them as triggers for a deliberate review and should re-estimate the relationships as new data accumulate.
